clue.text: Abbess and abbot are both in this order

definitions.text: Abbess and abbot are both in this order

parts.words: Abbess and abbot are both in this order
parts.note: the 'order' looks like a religious order for monks and nuns, but it is the sequence of letters: A, B, B, E, S, S and A, B, B, O, T each run from early to late in the alphabet

explanation.surface: A question about which religious order counts both an abbess and an abbot among its members.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Order' tempts you towards a monastic order; instead check the letters of each word, which never step backwards through the alphabet.
explanation.definitionFit: Letters arranged as they come in the alphabet are in alphabetical order, which both words happen to be.

clue.text: Foreign film's a new one on me

indicators.note: in a down clue, one piece placed on another sits above it, so the letters come before

parts.note: the Roman numeral for one is I
taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone admitting a foreign film is unfamiliar to them: 'that's a new one on me'.
explanation.walkthrough: 'a new one on me' reads as an idiom for something unfamiliar, but each word gives letters in turn.
explanation.definitionFit: Anime is Japanese animation, so to an English-speaking audience it is a kind of film from abroad.

clue.text: Monumental bit of stonework that's built up on Hampstead Heath

definitions.meaning: first meaning: a commemorative tablet fixed to a wall or monument

definitions.text: that's built up on Hampstead Heath
definitions.meaning: second meaning: the deposit that builds up on teeth; Hampstead Heath is Cockney rhyming slang for teeth

explanation.walkthrough: Hampstead Heath is a park in north London, but in Cockney rhyming slang it stands for teeth, so what builds up there is dental deposit.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means both a memorial tablet, like London's blue ones, and the film of bacteria that collects on teeth.

clue.text: One meant to receive tablets gets through Red Sea with God's backing, somehow

indicators.note: the tablets pass through the jumbled letters, so they end up sitting inside them
done in some way or other, so the letters are rearranged
the back of a word is its last letter

parts.note: E is slang for an ecstasy tablet, so tablets are ES

explanation.surface: Moses, meant to receive the tablets of the law, crosses the Red Sea with divine help.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface is all Exodus, but 'tablets' are ecstasy pills, ES. RED SEA plus D, the back of God, is rearranged as ADDRSEE, and ES goes through that.
explanation.definitionFit: An addressee is the person a letter or message is directed to, the intended recipient.

clue.text: All of Elis James' content revolves around some post found online

indicators.note: turning round means the letters run the other way, last to first
a word's content is what lies inside it, so each name loses its first and last letters

parts.note: the inside of Elis is LI
the inside of James is AME

explanation.surface: A comment that the comedian Elis James's material all circles round things people have posted online.
explanation.walkthrough: Elis James is a Welsh comedian and broadcaster; 'All of' tells you the same treatment applies to both names.
explanation.definitionFit: Email is electronic mail, messages sent over the internet, so it is a form of post found online.

clue.text: Unwanted guest less polite after putting away first unit of beer

indicators.note: the less polite word is placed after the trimmed beer measure
putting away the first letter means dropping the opening letter of the word

parts.note: a pint is the standard measure in which beer is served in a British pub
less polite means ruder

explanation.surface: A guest who gets ruder after downing their first pint of beer is no longer welcome.
explanation.walkthrough: 'putting away' suggests drinking the beer; here it means removing the opening letter of the measure.
explanation.definitionFit: An intruder is someone who comes in where they are not wanted, a guest nobody invited.

clue.text: Heading off injury, first sign of danger and I'll pop into a ball

definitions.text: Heading off injury, first sign of danger and I'll pop into a ball

indicators.note: taking the heading, or first letter, off the word

parts.note: harm means injury

indicators.note: these letters slip inside the other pair

parts.note: O looks like a ball

indicators.note: the first sign of a word is its opening letter

parts.note: first letter D
the apostrophe is ignored, giving ILL

explanation.surface: The animal speaks: to avoid harm, at the first hint of danger it rolls itself into a ball.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue is both the wordplay and the definition: ARM, then D and ILL popped into A and O.
explanation.definitionFit: The armadillo, an armoured mammal, famously curls into a tight ball to protect itself when threatened.

clue.text: Heartless killjoy getting annoyed as comic speaks

indicators.note: being riled or stirred up, so the letters are mixed up
without its heart, the central letter of the word being dropped

explanation.surface: A grumpy killjoy gets irritated by the way a comedian talks.
explanation.walkthrough: KILLJOY has seven letters, so its heart is the fourth, L; remove it to get KILJOY, then rearrange.
explanation.definitionFit: A comedian talks in a joking way, so the adverb describes how a comic speaks.

clue.text: Showing true colours, posh editor supports this paper but not the i

indicators.note: in a down clue, a supporting piece sits underneath and so comes last

parts.note: U means upper-class, as in U and non-U

indicators.note: except for, so the named letter is removed

parts.note: the Indy is the nickname of The Independent, the paper this crossword appears in
the letter I; the i is also the name of the Independent's sister paper

explanation.surface: A posh editor backs the Independent, minus its offshoot paper, the i, while being open about their views.
explanation.walkthrough: 'this paper' is the Independent, known as the Indy; removing the I leaves NDY.
explanation.definitionFit: Something undyed keeps its natural colour, so it shows its true colours literally.

clue.text: Means of contacting spook needs approval from Paris and Berlin

parts.note: oui is French for yes
ja is German for yes, as said in Berlin

explanation.surface: A séance tool needing sign-off from both the French and German authorities.
explanation.walkthrough: The board's name is said to come from the French and German words for yes.
explanation.definitionFit: A Ouija board is used in séances to receive supposed messages from ghosts.

clue.text: American making plans picked up board game piece

indicators.note: heard, so the word is replaced by one that sounds the same

parts.note: a draughtsman is a piece in draughts, the British name for checkers

explanation.surface: An American designer picks up a piece from a board game.
explanation.walkthrough: Draughts is the British name for checkers. The American spelling of a person who draws plans sounds the same as the British draughts piece.
explanation.definitionFit: A draftsman, in US spelling, produces technical drawings and plans.

clue.text: One dropped into Manhattan on way to diner, perhaps

definitions.text: One dropped into Manhattan on way to diner, perhaps

parts.words: One dropped into Manhattan on way to diner, perhaps
parts.note: a Manhattan is a cocktail, and a frozen block is dropped into it before it is served to the diner

explanation.walkthrough: Manhattan reads as New York; it is the whisky cocktail.
explanation.definitionFit: A small frozen block of water is dropped into a drink such as a cocktail to chill it.

clue.text: What's regularly clean and then wet again?

definitions.text: What's regularly clean and then wet again?

indicators.note: taking letters at regular intervals, here the second and fourth

parts.note: to undry something is, jokingly, to make it wet once more

explanation.surface: A riddle about something that keeps being cleaned and then soaked again.
explanation.walkthrough: 'undry' is a jokey coinage for making wet again. The whole clue also describes the washing, which is clean, then wet in the next wash.
explanation.definitionFit: Laundry is the clothes and linen that are washed, dried, and washed again in a cycle.

clue.text: Religious group rejecting Methuselah's creed and age, initially

indicators.note: rejected means sent back, so the letters are turned round

parts.note: Methuselah is the setter, so Methuselah's means my

indicators.note: the initial letters of the words named

explanation.surface: A church group refusing to accept the setter's beliefs and his great age, Methuselah being famously old.
explanation.walkthrough: Methuselah is the setter's pseudonym, so his possessions are MY; reversed this gives YM.
explanation.definitionFit: The YMCA, the Young Men's Christian Association, is a Christian organisation.

clue.text: Blender yielding a meal during tea-time

indicators.note: within, so the other letters go inside

parts.note: cha is slang for tea
an eon is a long period of time

indicators.note: giving up, so the meal surrenders the letter

explanation.surface: A kitchen blender producing a meal at teatime.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Blender' looks like a kitchen gadget, but it is an animal that blends into its background. 'yielding a' tells the meal to give up its A.
explanation.definitionFit: A chameleon changes colour to merge with its surroundings, so it is something that blends in.

clue.text: Primitive vehicle stuck outside cabin shifted with tool

indicators.note: placed around, so the vehicle's letters go round the other word

parts.note: a sled is a simple vehicle on runners
a hovel is a rough hut or cabin

explanation.surface: A sledge stuck outside a cabin was moved by digging, as in snow.
explanation.walkthrough: SLED goes outside HOVEL to give S + HOVEL + LED.
explanation.definitionFit: Shovelled describes moving earth or snow with a spade-like implement.

clue.text: Attack of giggles possibly showing Bottom up in middle of June, for example?

indicators.note: the moved letters go inside the trimmed word
keeping only the middle, so the outer letters are dropped

parts.note: June is an example of a month

indicators.note: in a down clue the bottom letter is brought up to the top

parts.note: giggles are one kind of laughs

explanation.surface: A fit of giggles at Bottom, the comic weaver in A Midsummer Night's Dream, a play set around midsummer in June.
explanation.walkthrough: Bottom looks like Shakespeare's character; in a down clue it is the last letter of the word, which moves to the top.
explanation.definitionFit: An onslaught is a fierce assault, an all-out attack.

clue.text: Little thing wriggling around in utero without name

indicators.note: used in its old sense of outside, so the shuffled letters go round the other one
moving restlessly, so the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A tiny baby squirming in the womb, yet to be given a name.
explanation.walkthrough: 'without' reads as lacking, but here it means outside: the anagram of IN UTERO wraps round N.
explanation.definitionFit: A neutrino is a subatomic particle with almost no mass, a tiny thing even by particle standards.

clue.text: Star celeb misplacing accessories …

indicators.note: putting things in the wrong place, so the letters are reordered

explanation.surface: A famous celebrity keeps losing their jewellery.
explanation.definitionFit: Bracelets are jewellery worn round the wrist, a common kind of fashion accessory.

clue.text: Cheeky underwear getting Frenchman's nose up

parts.note: a bra is an item of underwear

indicators.note: in a down clue, going up means reading from bottom to top

parts.note: nez is French for nose

explanation.surface: A cheeky item of lingerie makes a Frenchman turn his nose up.
explanation.definitionFit: Brazen means bold and shameless, which is close to cheeky or impudent.

clue.text: … did sport with next to nothing on

indicators.note: placed beside, so the pieces join up side by side

parts.note: O looks like zero, nothing
re means about or on, as in a letter's subject

explanation.surface: Continuing from the previous clue, the star celeb played some sport wearing almost nothing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'did sport' reads as playing a game; here sport means to wear, as in sporting a hat.
explanation.definitionFit: To sport something is to wear it showily, so having worn an item is having sported it.

clue.text: City player coming off, according to commentator

indicators.note: what a commentator says is heard, so the word is said aloud

parts.note: a player leaving the pitch is an exiter, one who exits

explanation.surface: A sports commentator reports a footballer being substituted in a city match.
explanation.walkthrough: Exeter is a cathedral city in Devon, England; 'exiter' is a jokey coinage for one who exits.
explanation.definitionFit: Exeter is a cathedral city in south-west England, the county town of Devon.

clue.text: One armed and dangerous person has it in for you, we hear

indicators.note: the person takes on new letters
put in place of, so one piece substitutes for another

parts.note: a human is a person

indicators.note: said aloud, the word sounds like a single letter

parts.note: said aloud, you sounds like the letter U
taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone holding a grudge against you might be a dangerous armed killer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'has it in for you' reads as an idiom for bearing a grudge; literally, the word for a person has IT in place of U.
explanation.definitionFit: A hitman is a paid assassin, who carries a weapon and is dangerous.

clue.text: Old record used in Act I's clumsily cleaned up for theatre

indicators.note: placed inside, so the record's letters go into the others
done awkwardly, so the letters are jumbled

parts.note: an EP, an extended-play record, is an old vinyl format

explanation.surface: A vintage record is played in the first act of a stage show.
explanation.walkthrough: 'theatre' suggests the stage; it is an operating theatre, where everything must be sterile.
explanation.definitionFit: Aseptic means free from germs, as instruments and rooms must be for surgery.

clue.text: Twitter CEO helped its rivals prosper at first

indicators.note: the first letters of the words named

explanation.surface: The boss of the social network Twitter once helped competing firms do well.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Twitter' looks like the social network, but here it is a bird's twittering.
explanation.definitionFit: A chirp is the short high call of a bird, and a twitter is a series of such calls.

clue.text: Fat cat abandoned by banks poised to be banged up

indicators.note: the banks are the sides of the word, so only its middle remains
knocked about, so the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A fat cat, a greedy rich executive, is deserted by the banks and is about to be jailed.
explanation.walkthrough: Banged up is British slang for put in prison; here it shuffles A from 'cat' with POISED.
explanation.definitionFit: Adipose is the technical adjective for body fat, as in adipose tissue.

clue.text: Watering hole gets locals tipsy on a regular basis

indicators.note: every other letter, picked out at regular intervals

explanation.surface: A pub, or watering hole, makes its regulars drunk again and again.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Watering hole' looks like a pub, which fits the tipsy locals; here it is a desert spring.
explanation.definitionFit: An oasis is a fertile spot in a desert with water, where animals and travellers drink.

clue.text: European member is in government doing woeful work

parts.note: a leg is a limb, a member of the body

explanation.surface: A European politician in government is doing a terrible job.
explanation.walkthrough: 'woeful work' reads as poor performance; it is a mournful poem.
explanation.definitionFit: To elegise is to write an elegy, a sorrowful poem lamenting the dead.

clue.text: Shot that might be seen in frame during Christmas season

definitions.text: Shot that might be seen in frame

indicators.note: within, so the letters are found inside the words that follow

explanation.surface: A photograph taken over the festive period might appear in a picture frame.
explanation.walkthrough: 'frame' suggests a picture; it is a frame of snooker, and the shot is a sharply swerving cue stroke.
explanation.definitionFit: A massé is a billiards or snooker stroke played with a near-vertical cue to make the ball curve.

clue.text: Poor workers getting mistreated (con men set it up, bypassing union)

indicators.note: handled badly, so the letters are rearranged
going round without, so one letter is left out of the jumble

explanation.surface: Low-paid staff exploited by fraudsters who set up a scheme without any trade union.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Poor workers' reads as underpaid staff; it means workers who are no good. Take U from the letters of CON MEN SET IT UP and rearrange the rest.
explanation.definitionFit: Incompetents are people lacking the skill to do their job properly.
